images.alt: A black-and-white photograph of a crowd of children on a city street. Girls in dresses hold hands in a ring around a smiling boy who sits on the ground holding a stick, while more children stand watching behind them.
images.caption: Children playing a ring game on a New York 'play street', 1910
images.credit: Bain News Service, 1910. Library of Congress, via Wikimedia Commons
images.note: Glass-plate negative; some lifting of the emulsion shows as a pale outline around the girls on the left. Cropped only to remove the negative's black border and handwritten title.

images.alt: A painting of three young women in grey silk dresses with pink sashes sitting around a small card table, each holding a hand of playing cards, with flowering azaleas and a black lacquered screen behind them.
images.caption: Hearts are Trumps: three sisters at the card table, by John Everett Millais, Britain, 1872
images.credit: John Everett Millais, 1872. Tate Britain, via Wikimedia Commons

images.alt: A hand-coloured postcard of a country school with long timber buildings and verandahs under a pale sky. Groups of children run and play on the grassy, dusty playground in front. The words 'The State School, Southport, Q.' are printed at the top.
images.caption: Children playing in the playground of Southport State School, Queensland, about 1908
images.credit: Unknown photographer, about 1908 (hand-coloured postcard). State Library of Queensland, via Wikimedia Commons
images.note: Australian, as requested, but only about 1000 px wide at the source, so the hero is 960 px wide and the children are small. A higher-resolution non-Australian alternative would be a Bain News Service New York street photograph.

images.alt: A painting of a crowded schoolroom with whitewashed walls and a map of the world. An old schoolmaster in spectacles peers from his desk while about twenty children sit on benches, read, whisper and laugh. On the right a woman in a bonnet points as she brings in a boy in a red waistcoat, other children peep in at the door, and a writing slate leans against a stool at the front.
images.caption: A mother brings a new pupil to a crowded schoolroom, painted by Thomas Brooks, Britain, 1854
images.credit: Thomas Brooks, 1854. Image from the Dorotheum auction house, via Wikimedia Commons
images.note: Catalogued at auction under the German title 'Der neue Schüler' (The New Pupil); signed and dated 1854.

images.alt: A hand-coloured board game printed as a spiral track of 67 numbered spaces. Many spaces have small pictures of people standing for good and bad behaviour, and the centre picture at space 67 shows the Mansion of Happiness, with figures in a garden beneath an eagle and a banner.
images.caption: The Mansion of Happiness board, published by W. & S. B. Ives, Salem, Massachusetts, 1843
images.credit: W. & S. B. Ives (publishers), lithograph by B. W. Thayer & Co., 1843. Library of Congress, via Wikimedia Commons
images.note: Cropped to remove the library's colour bar and scanning background. The original scan is 1446 px wide, so the hero is 1327 px wide.

images.alt: Two pages of an old Chinese book printed in black ink on brown paper. Each page shows four figures, several of them people, built from the seven tangram pieces; faint shapes show through from the other side of the thin paper.
images.caption: Pages from Qiqiao xinpu, a Chinese tangram puzzle book, in a copy the library dates to 1816
images.credit: Unknown author, Qiqiao xinpu (Ch'i ch'iao hsin p'u), Fu Wen Tang, dated 1816 in the library record. Princeton Theological Seminary Library, via the Internet Archive
images.note: Two single-page scans (Internet Archive pages n166 and n165) placed side by side and trimmed; they may not be a true facing opening. The Internet Archive item carries no rights statement; the book is public domain by age. The 1818 French caricature on Commons is only 756 px wide, and the 1818 French book 'Casse-tête, ou Enigmes chinoises' (Gallica) has only thin line diagrams, so this bolder Chinese book was preferred.

images.alt: An old brown-toned photograph of a girl in a checked dress leaning on a low wooden table with a draughts board and moving a piece, while a boy in a dark velvet jacket sits on the other side with his eyes closed. A third child's legs show at the right edge.
images.caption: Two children of the Denman family playing draughts, photographed by Lewis Carroll (date unknown)
images.credit: Lewis Carroll (Charles L. Dodgson), date unknown. Mario Trevisan collection, via Wikimedia Commons
images.note: Commons gives no date for the photograph itself (Carroll photographed between 1856 and 1880). The names on Commons ('Charlotte Edith Denman, Arthur Denman and Grace Denman's legs') are ambiguous about which child is which, so the caption does not name them.

images.alt: A painting of a lively kitchen. A blindfolded girl in a white dress reaches out with both arms while other children dodge, hide and laugh around her: a girl in pink leans away, a boy has tumbled to the floor, a father smokes a pipe by the fireplace and a mother sits holding a baby.
images.caption: Blind Man's Buff, a family guessing game, painted by John Lewis Krimmel, 1814
images.credit: John Lewis Krimmel, 1814. Terra Foundation for American Art, via Wikimedia Commons
images.note: Shows Blind Man's Buff, a different parlour game in which the blindfolded player must guess whom they have caught; no good public-domain image of Twenty Questions itself was found.

images.alt: Four old playing cards side by side on a dark background, each a hand-coloured drawing of a bird-headed character: Le Docteur in a tall black hat, La Femme du Docteur in a bonnet and green dress, Le Fils du Docteur with a yellow beak, and La Fille du Docteur in purple. A small bottle emblem is in the top corner of each card.
images.caption: The Doctor's family from a French 'happy families' game (jeu de sept familles), drawn by André Gill, 1876
images.credit: André Gill, 1876. Bibliothèque nationale de France (Gallica)
images.note: Not the Jaques game: the only Jaques Happy Families image on Commons is 435 px wide, and the V&A's Tenniel-attributed set is not freely licensed. These are four separate card scans (Gallica views 19, 21, 23 and 25) trimmed and arranged by us on a plain dark background; the arrangement and background are not historical.

images.alt: A painting of a classroom of small children in smocks at long wooden desks. Some write with pens in exercise books, others write on small framed slates, a teacher bends over a pupil at the back, and a reading chart hangs on the green wall.
images.caption: Young pupils writing in exercise books and on slates in a French classroom, painted by Jean Geoffroy, 1889
images.credit: Henri Jules Jean Geoffroy, 1889. Via Wikimedia Commons
images.note: Title 'En classe, le travail des petits'. Shows writing slates (as used for noughts and crosses), not the game itself; the holding institution is not stated on Commons. The source file is 1500 px wide.

images.alt: A painting of five children around a wooden table in a sunny room. A girl in a white dress with long plaits reaches for the cards in the middle, a boy holds a card up high, and the others clutch their hands of cards and watch closely.
images.caption: Children playing cards at a table by a window, painted by the Swedish artist Hugo Salmson (before 1894)
images.credit: Hugo Salmson, date unknown (before 1894). Private collection, via Wikimedia Commons
images.note: The painting does not say which card game is being played. Commons dates it 'by 1894' (the painter died that year) and gives no original source.

images.alt: A sepia photograph of a group of boys in caps, jackets and knee breeches on a dirt street. One boy kneels to flick a marble towards a small cluster of marbles on the ground while the others stand or bend over to watch; wooden houses and a bare tree are behind them.
images.caption: Boys who worked in the cotton mill playing marbles in Salisbury, North Carolina, photographed by Lewis Hine, 1908
images.credit: Lewis Wickes Hine, 1908. National Child Labor Committee Collection, Library of Congress, via Wikimedia Commons
images.note: Hine's original caption names the boy shooting as Henry Dedman, a warper who had worked in the mill for five years.

images.alt: A black-and-white photograph of four children by a wooden fence in a bare yard. A boy hops on one foot across a long hopscotch court marked in white on the ground, a girl stands on the court, and two boys watch from the far end, one pointing.
images.caption: Children playing hopscotch on a court marked on bare ground, photographed in 1891
images.credit: Fellows Photographic Co., 1891. Library of Congress, via Wikimedia Commons
images.note: One half of a stereograph copyrighted in 1891 by the Fellows Photographic Co. (Library of Congress cph.3b02655), cropped to remove the arched mount and printed caption. The place is not recorded. Only the 1280 px Commons thumbnail could be downloaded, so the hero is 1228 px wide.

images.alt: A painting of a young woman in a striped jacket and blue apron tossing a small ball into the air with one hand and watching it, with small knucklebones lying on the table in front of her.
images.caption: The Game of Knucklebones by the French painter Jean-Siméon Chardin, 1734
images.credit: Jean-Siméon Chardin, 1734. Baltimore Museum of Art, via Wikimedia Commons
images.note: Upright painting; the hero is 1280 x 1543 px. The banner focus keeps the ball, hand and face; the knucklebones on the table only show in the full picture.

images.alt: A black-and-white press photograph of a tree-lined avenue where a line of boys run towards the camera, each driving a large hoop with a stick, while a crowd of men, women and children in hats watches from behind.
images.caption: Boys racing hoops at a hoop championship at the Porte de Courcelles, Paris, 22 October 1911
images.credit: Agence Rol, 1911. Bibliothèque nationale de France (Gallica), via Wikimedia Commons
images.note: Cropped to remove the glass negative's border, numbers and handwritten title.

images.alt: A black-and-white photograph of a smiling girl in a wide-brimmed hat and loose dress skipping on one foot on a sunny gravel path, her rope swinging behind her. A uniformed man with medals walks nearby, and women and children sit under the trees behind.
images.caption: A girl skipping along a path in a public garden, June 1913, photographed by the Paris agency Agence Rol
images.credit: Agence Rol, 1913. Bibliothèque nationale de France (Gallica), via Wikimedia Commons
images.note: The BnF record does not name the garden or town. Cropped to remove the glass negative's border, numbers and handwritten title.

images.alt: A black-and-white etching of shiny horse chestnuts lying with their split, spiky cases and dry leaves on a table. A short French verse is written in the lower right corner and the title 'Marrons d'Inde' is printed underneath.
images.caption: Marrons d'Inde: horse chestnuts (conkers) and their spiky cases, etching by Alfred Taiée, Paris, about 1875
images.credit: Alfred Taiée, about 1875 (published by Cadart & Luce, Paris). Wellcome Collection
images.note: Shows the horse chestnuts used for conkers, not the game. Wellcome Collection marks this image with the Public Domain Mark (the Commons copy is tagged CC BY 4.0 from an older Wellcome upload). The verse reads, roughly: 'Under your prickly shell, conker, why hide so well, when everyone knows you're worth nothing!'

images.alt: A painting of three gentlemen in powdered wigs and embroidered coats in a room hung with a tapestry. One man leans forward playing with a cup-and-ball toy, another sits watching, a third stands holding a cup-and-ball behind his back, and a dropped cup-and-ball lies on the floor.
images.caption: Gentlemen in 18th-century dress playing bilboquet (cup and ball), painted by Louis Monziès, about 1880
images.credit: Louis Monziès, about 1880 (date uncertain). Image from the Dorotheum auction house, via Wikimedia Commons
images.note: German auction title 'Die Bilboquet-Spieler' (The Bilboquet Players); Commons gives the date as 'circa 1880 (?)'.
